path.title: Data engineering foundations
path.summary: Loads that survive retries: idempotent writes and incremental extraction with a watermark.

lessons.title: Idempotent loads: safe to run twice
lessons.summary: Design a load so that running it again gives the same table: upsert on a key, replace a partition, and never append blindly.

blocks.title: Why reruns happen
blocks.body: Schedulers retry failed tasks, operators rerun a day by hand and a source can deliver the same file twice. A load is idempotent when running it once or several times with the same input leaves the target in the same state. Then a retry is always safe.

blocks.title: Three idempotent patterns
blocks.body: Upsert on a business key: update the rows whose key exists, insert the others (MERGE INTO in SQL, a unique_key incremental model in dbt). Replace a whole partition (one day, one file) with a delete-then-insert or an overwrite in one transaction. Insert only the keys that are not there yet (an anti join). A plain INSERT of the batch is not idempotent: the second run doubles the rows. The example computes an upsert result with SELECT, so it changes nothing.

blocks.title: The key decides
blocks.body: Idempotency needs a key that identifies a row of the source: an order id, or (order_id, line_no). Deduplicate the batch on that key first (keep the latest version), or the upsert finds two candidates for one target row.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: Predict the rows after applying the batch once. Then imagine replacing target with the result and applying the same batch again: which rows change?

steps.title: Target and batch
steps.body: The target has ids 1 to 3; the batch updates id 2 and adds id 4.

steps.title: The batch wins for its keys
steps.body: Every batch row goes to the result: Ben now lives in Paris and Dina is new.

steps.title: Untouched rows stay
steps.body: Target rows whose id is not in the batch are kept as they were.

steps.title: Run it twice
steps.body: Apply the same batch to the result: the output is identical. Appending the batch instead would give two rows for id 2 on every run.

lessons.title: Incremental loads with a watermark
lessons.summary: Load only what changed since the last run with a high watermark, reread a lookback window for late rows, and keep the write idempotent.

blocks.title: Full versus incremental
blocks.body: A full load rereads the whole source on every run: simple and always correct, but its cost grows with the table. An incremental load reads only the rows changed since the last successful run, found with a watermark: the highest updated_at (or sequence number) already loaded, stored by the pipeline.

blocks.title: The watermark rule
blocks.body: Select updated_at > the stored watermark; on the first run, when no watermark exists yet, select everything. Store the new watermark (the highest updated_at actually loaded) only after the load has committed, so a failed run is retried from the old value.

blocks.title: Late and equal timestamps
blocks.body: A row can be committed in the source after a later timestamp was already read, and several rows can share the watermark value. Reread a small lookback window (updated_at > watermark - interval) and write with an upsert on the key, so rows read twice change nothing.

blocks.title: Deletes and backfills
blocks.body: A watermark on updated_at never sees a hard delete: use soft deletes, a change data capture feed or a periodic full comparison. A backfill reruns the load for a past range with explicit bounds instead of the stored watermark.

blocks.title: Before you run
blocks.body: Predict the rows selected with the stored watermark. Then remove the watermark row and predict the first-run result.

code.source:
WITH source_rows(id, updated_at) AS (
  VALUES (1, TIMESTAMP '2026-10-01 08:00'), (2, TIMESTAMP '2026-10-02 09:30'),
         (3, TIMESTAMP '2026-10-02 23:59'), (4, TIMESTAMP '2026-10-03 07:15')
), watermark(table_name, loaded_until) AS (
  VALUES ('source_rows', TIMESTAMP '2026-10-02 09:30')
)
SELECT s.id, s.updated_at
FROM source_rows s
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM watermark w WHERE w.table_name = 'source_rows')
   OR s.updated_at > (SELECT w.loaded_until FROM watermark w WHERE w.table_name = 'source_rows')
ORDER BY s.updated_at;

steps.title: The stored watermark
steps.body: The last run loaded everything up to 2026-10-02 09:30.

steps.title: First run
steps.body: Without a watermark row, NOT EXISTS is true and every row is selected.

steps.title: Only newer rows
steps.body: With the watermark, rows 3 and 4 are selected. Row 2 equals the watermark and was already loaded.

steps.title: Advance after commit
steps.body: After the write commits, store 2026-10-03 07:15 as the new watermark. A failed run keeps the old one and is retried safely.
